articles.title: George W Bush raises money for Republicans, but not key Senate candidate
articles.summary: George W. Bush hosted a fundraiser for Senate Republicans but notably excluded Ken Paxton, who defeated Bush's nephew in the 2022 Texas primary.
articles.body: Former President George W. Bush is helping fundraise for Republicans, but not the one who defeated his nephew, George P. Bush, in the 2022 Republican primary for Texas attorney general. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, held a fundraiser Monday night for Maintain the Majority with the former president as a "special guest," The New York Times reported. The event did not include GOP Senate candidate and current Texas AG Ken Paxton, who defeated Cornyn in this year's primary. Maintain the Majority is a PAC that lists Cornyn along with Sens. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska; Jon Husted, R-Ohio, Susan Collins, R-Maine; Michigan Sen.-nominee Mike Rogers, New Hampshire Sen.-nominee John E. Sununu; and Iowa Sen.-nominee Ashley Hinson as joint fund participants, Minnesota Republican Sen.-nominee Michele Tafoya was a late addition to the Monday night event, according to the Times. Notably absent on that list are Paxton, Republican Georgia Sen.-nominee Mike Collins and Republican North Carolina Sen.-nominee Michael Whatley, a trio of Senate candidates closely tied to Trump's political orbit. TRUMP FLEXES HIS POLITICAL MUSCLE OVER GOP AS DEMOCRATS SEE MIDTERM OPENING IN KEY RED STATE Bush and Cornyn have long had a complicated relationship with President Donald Trump and his favored candidates, like Paxton. Karl Rove, a former senior presidential advisor to Bush, recently declared he would vote for a Texas Democrat, too. THUNE-ALIGNED GROUPS UNLEASH HISTORIC WAR CHEST TO DEFEND SENATE MAJORITY: 'WINNING MESSAGE' "Early voting in Texas starts Monday, October 19, 2026 (28 days from today, September 21)," a Cornyn X post on Monday morning read, notably leaving out a mention of Paxton. "It runs through Friday, October 30. The 2026 midterms (Election Day) are Tuesday, November 3, 2026 — 43 days from today." While the PAC funds might not include Paxton, Trump's own midterm campaign war chest at MAGA Inc. — now under the watchful eye of former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt — has more than $415 million cash on hand, according to the latest FEC filing reported Sunday. Michigan, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine and Alaska are all rated toss-ups in the latest Fox News Power Rankings in the race to hold the Republican's slim 53-47 Senate majority. Democrats are looking at flipping seats against Collins, Husted, Sullivan, Hinson in Iowa, Whatley in North Carolina and Paxton in Texas. Republicans are eyeing potential pickups in Michigan, New Hampshire and Georgia. REPUBLICAN CAVALRY ARRIVES FOR KEN PAXTON AS BIG-BUCKS TEXAS OFFENSIVE OPENS CASH FLOODGATES While midterms are historically unfavorable to the political party seated in the White House, Republicans holding the Senate could help tamp down Democrat momentum in Trump's final two years in office if the slim 218-214 Republican House majority is lost. While Cornyn's establishment Republican coffers might not be made available to the man who ousted him in the primary, Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters has been confident that Texas' Senate seat will remain in the GOP's hands. "You got to remember Ken Paxton won this state a couple of times in the general – he won a primary against a strong incumbent that's been there for a long time by a couple hundred thousand votes," Gruters told Fox News Digital last month. "People want this race to be the biggest race in the country, but it really won't be because, at the end of the day, Paxton has proven time and time again that he's a winner; he's a winner in this state. Texas is ruby red," Gruters said. "Texas is a hardcore Republican state. They're going to send up a MAGA warrior because we have a lot of work to do, including passing the Save America Act." JOHN THUNE GOES 'ALL IN' FOR KEN PAXTON AFTER BITTER PRIMARY RIPPED GOP APART CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP While Texas is seeing California liberals flock to the state, Gruters predicted Paxton's statewide campaign strength is going to hold against Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico. "Texas is a massive state, a lot resources from California are pouring in because these California liberals like Talafreako, but I don't think it's going to help him at the end of the day," Gruters added. "Paxton is going to win this race."

articles.title: Rubio defends Trump’s banning media organizations, arguing there aren’t ‘soldiers kicking down the doors’ of the outlets
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the Trump administration’s decision to bar three media organizations from the White House, saying in an interview on NBC News’ “TODAY” that President Donald Trump was not closing outlets or arresting reporters.
articles.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the Trump administration’s decision to bar three media organizations from the White House, saying in an interview on NBC News’ “TODAY” that President Donald Trump was not closing outlets or arresting reporters. “We’re not closing CNN,” Rubio said of the ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico. “There aren’t a bunch of police officers or soldiers kicking down the doors of MSNBC or MS NOW, whatever it’s called, and arresting people and unplugging it from the grid. They’re just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House.” In the Tuesday interview, Rubio also addressed the war with Iran, including its impact on oil and gas prices, arguing that if Tehran were allowed to develop a nuclear weapon, it would use the threat to constrain oil shipments and drive prices up even further. He also discussed concerns about the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and the need for a developmental framework to maintain the benefits of the technology while lowering the risks. Trump’s ban on the media outlets marked the president’s most extreme instance so far of blocking access for news organizations whose coverage he dislikes. The three banned outlets sued the Trump administration Monday, and major television networks, including NBC News, refused to provide TV pool coverage of the president at least through Monday. Pool coverage allows media members and subscribers to share video, editorial information and costs for newsworthy events where space is limited. Individual TV networks, including NBC News, continue to provide coverage of White House events that are open to the press, outside of the pool. Outside of events, NBC News reporters continue to report on the administration’s activities. Television pool coverage of other administration officials, including Rubio, has continued. On Monday, CNN provided TV pool coverage of him. When asked by “TODAY” host Craig Melvin whether he planned to make changes to his pool coverage, Rubio said, “We haven’t discussed it.” Rubio told “TODAY” that the three banned outlets would be able to continue covering the president from outside the White House, adding that Trump believed that the outlets have shown bias against his administration and therefore did not have a right to remain in the White House building. “What he is arguing is, why should I have these people, what right do they have to be embedded in this building?” Rubio said. “They can cover the White House. They just can’t have a desk there.” In their lawsuit, the outlets argued that the ban violated their due process and First Amendment rights, claiming the ban “retaliates against protected newsgathering and speech” and bars the outlets “from a nonpublic forum for unlawful reasons.” In his Truth Social announcement of the ban last week, Trump said the move was “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” In a separate post Monday, Trump again criticized media as “fake news,” calling it “a threat to our National Security” that “must be stopped.” Trump is set to address world leaders Tuesday at the United Nations General Assembly, followed by a high-stakes summit in Washington, D.C., with Chinese President Xi Jinping later this week. Iran war impact Asked whether Trump plans to meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who will attend the assembly, Rubio said Trump “has said that he’s open a meeting with anybody.” Trump said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday that he would “probably” be open to meeting the Iranian president. Iran’s president is an important official of the country, but not the top official. The top Iranian official, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, has not been seen in public since taking over the position in March after his father, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in airstrikes at the start of the war. The war with Iran has sent economic effects rippling around the world, and the cost of oil and gas has spiked since the conflict began. An NBC News poll found that 62% of registered voters think the war has not been worth the costs. Pressed on rising prices and Americans’ sentiment on the war, Rubio said that “anyone who’s concerned about prices itself is not wrong.” “Obviously, if the war is being blamed for that, then of course you’re going to hear and you’re going to see responses like that,” he said, referring to the polling. Rubio argued, however, that prices would be far higher if Iran had a nuclear weapon and could “choke off the world’s energy supply any time they wanted.” Concerns about AI Later this week, artificial intelligence is expected to be a major topic at the Trump-Xi summit. Concerns about the future of AI have risen in recent weeks after industry insiders warned of potentially catastrophic impacts of the technology. Trump has argued for maintaining the accelerated development of AI in the U.S., saying it is necessary to ensure that America keeps its lead on the technology over global rivals like China. At one point, he posted on social media that the only guardrail needed for AI is “is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Rubio said in his interview Tuesday that the reality of AI is that the technology cannot be stopped. “Like every technological advance in human history, it’s impossible to stop it,” he said. “It will happen. The question is, how can we put guardrails and frameworks around it so that we can get the benefits of AI while mitigating the risks?” Rubio did not propose specific guardrails or frameworks, saying, “I don’t think anyone has an easy answer” for AI yet.

articles.title: Loomer says she’s ‘pissed’ at Trump for meeting Mamdani
articles.summary: Far-right commentator Laura Loomer lashed out Monday after President Trump praised New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) during a cordial press conference at Gracie Mansion ahead of Tuesday’s United Nations General Assembly in the city. “I’m pissed off,” Loomer wrote on the social platform X shortly after Trump met with Mamdani, who is New…
articles.body:
Far-right commentator Laura Loomer lashed out Monday after President Trump praised New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) during a cordial press conference at Gracie Mansion ahead of Tuesday’s United Nations General Assembly in the city.

“I’m pissed off,” Loomer wrote on the social platform X shortly after Trump met with Mamdani, who is New York City’s first Muslim mayor.

“We work so hard to combat the radical left and the anti-American Islamic jihadists who work to destroy our country everyday,” she said. “And for what? So they can be rewarded?”

Loomer, a staunch Trump ally who has informally advised the president, did not name Mamdani specifically in the post but has separately labeled the New York City mayor as an “Islamic jihadist” in the past.

Trump met with Mamdani at the mayor’s official residence Monday ahead of the U.N.’s annual gathering, continuing an unexpectedly friendly relationship between the two political rivals.

Trump described Gracie Mansion as one of his “favorite places in the World.”

The president and the mayor met privately for roughly an hour before appearing together before reporters, where Trump said he wanted Mamdani to succeed despite their political differences.

“I certainly hope he will be a great mayor,” Trump told reporters at the press conference. “I want what’s good for New York. I want what’s good for the country.”

“I want him to be a great mayor, and he’s certainly got potential, got great potential,” he added.

The two discussed immigration, affordability and a potential housing development at Sunnyside Yard in Queens, which would likely require federal approvals and funding.

Mamdani said he would continue working with the Trump administration so the two sides could deliver results for New Yorkers.

Trump and Mamdani have frequently clashed over the mayor’s progressive policies. Trump repeatedly attacked Mamdani during last year’s mayoral race, but the pair struck a surprisingly warm tone when Mamdani, then mayor-elect, visited the White House in November.

articles.title: Fox News Power Rankings: For the Democrats, where could it possibly go wrong?
articles.summary: Democrats hold an 11-point generic ballot lead as Trump's Iran war drives gas prices up 50%, dragging down Republican midterm prospects nationwide.
articles.body: From the moment President Donald Trump completed his comeback in 2024, voters had good reason to think that the Democrats would retake the House this November. The president’s party has lost ground in all but two elections since 1934, including the two Trump-era midterms, where the party in power lost 40 seats (Republicans, 2018) and 9 seats (Democrats, 2022). REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOUSE CONTROL COULD HINGE ON WHETHER THE OLD POLITICAL RULES STILL APPLY With Republicans currently hanging by a thread in the House, most of the work has already been done for Team Blue. The number of seats that will change hands is another question, and here, Trump’s signature policies are playing a big role. As we enter fall, Democrats are enjoying their widest polling lead of the year. Voters say they prefer the Democrat to the Republican in their district by an average of 7 points in new polls (49%-42%). LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN Democrats perform even better among likely voters, with an 11-point average lead (53%-42%). That’s a larger and more consistent lead than the GOP had this time four years ago. These polls suggest that we’re heading for a "blue wave" like the one Democrats rode eight years ago. (That wave probably won’t rise as high as it once did. Thanks to redistricting, there are fewer seats in play for either party, so think of a gain of a few dozen as the modern equivalent of 40.) Still, there are six weeks until Election Day, and there are some things we don’t know. With all signs currently pointing to a good Democratic night, where could it possibly go wrong? Will anything change on Iran? The administration’s decision to go to war with Iran is proving costly for the GOP. RECORD GAS PRICES SQUEEZE AMERICANS AS SUMMER TRAVEL SEASON ENDS, MIDTERMS LOOM AND IRAN WAR WAGES ON Gas prices sit at $4.48 today, up 50% from $2.98 at the start of the war, and increasing at a higher rate this month. Trump’s worst ratings have been on inflation and the cost of living, and 61% of voters called gas prices a "major problem" in last week’s Fox News Poll. Yesterday, Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson became the second Republican Senate candidate to call for an end to the war (the first was Sen. Susan Collins, in April). No doubt many vulnerable House GOP incumbents feel the same way. In an election that looks less like an embrace of Democrats than a rejection of Trump’s agenda, a change of course in Iran would have an impact. Could the DSA drag down the Democratic vote? Democrats have presented voters with two economic visions: the first, championed by candidates like Abdul El-Sayed and Troy Jackson, calls for a revolution on healthcare and taxes. The other, more common and less sweeping, is largely about undoing the Trump agenda. MORNING GLORY: FIVE SENATE RACES SHOW WHY DEMOCRATS MAY REGRET THEIR PRIMARY CHOICES Voters say they like core parts of the progressive agenda, including raising taxes on billionaires, which makes voters more likely to vote for a candidate by a 34-point margin, according to a new NBC News Poll, and "Medicare-for-all," which has a 17-point margin. But the movements to which those policies are tied don’t fare as well: voters are less likely to support a candidate endorsed by Bernie Sanders by a 10-point margin, and less likely to vote for a candidate who supports the Democratic Socialists of America by 19 points. We don’t know yet whether candidates on the left wing of the Democratic Party will be able to thread this needle. Trump’s economic messaging is broadly unpopular, according to the same poll, including his proposal to send $5,000 checks to voters if Republicans keep control of Congress, as well as sending funding and weapons to Israel. That’s what is likely to get Democrats over the line. But watch whether the DSA hurts the Dems. Are there more MAGA votes out there? The Republicans’ midterm convention is now in the rear-view mirror, and it didn’t make a dent in the polls we’ve seen. That probably wasn’t the goal for the GOP, who used the "Trumpapalooza" to remind loyal MAGA voters about the president’s wins on immigration and crime, among other issues. How many of them will show up on Election Day? In last week’s Fox News Poll, a quarter of voters said an endorsement from President Trump makes them more likely to vote for a candidate. That quarter is mostly the MAGA base, and it’s large enough to impact a race. MAGA turnout could limit the Democrats’ ceiling. In this week’s Power Rankings, Kansas’ Senate race gets more competitive and 17 House races shift toward the Democrats. Plus, updates in two gubernatorial races. Senate: Kansas becomes the ninth battleground state Democrats can celebrate a shift in the political environment, but every Senate race is different. It’s still a toss-up in this forecast. Each party has 47 seats, with six in the middle to determine control: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. Races in the "lean" categories are highly competitive, too, and today, Kansas joins New Hampshire and North Carolina to round out the list of nine battleground states. Kansas has been on the Democrats’ radar for most of the year, thanks to what they believe to be a star recruit in megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton. He is campaigning on gas and diesel prices, which have an outsize impact in the rural and agriculture-heavy Midwest. Sen. Roger Marshall, the incumbent, got some help last week from a star of the Republicans’ own: Vice President JD Vance, who rallied with Marshall to promote the Trump administration’s manufacturing agenda. The state hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years, but it isn’t allergic to statewide Dems: incumbent governor Laura Kelly is one, and she won in both 2018 and 2022. Kansas moves from Likely R to Lean R. Meanwhile, in Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is consolidating support as he seeks a second term. His race moves from Lean D to Likely D. House: Democrats enjoy a higher ceiling; narrow pathways remain for a Republican majority The Democrats have made bigger gains in the House, where this week’s set of polls has the most impact. The party has 215 seats in this forecast, which means they would only need to win 3 of the 19 toss-ups to flip the House. On a "good night" for Democrats, which would see them win all of those toss-up races, they’d take up to 234 seats, leaving the Republicans with 201. Narrow pathways remain for the GOP. While this forecast sees an expansion of the Republican House majority as unlikely, a good night for the party would have them hold on to the House with 220 seats. The shifts are largely a product of the generic ballot polling. The Democrats’ lead among likely voters of 8 to 13 points will be too much for GOP campaigns in some highly competitive areas to overcome. The same is true even for a few districts that Trump won by a healthy margin two years ago. These changes also reflect the shift among Hispanic voters toward Democrats: from D+12 in the 2024 presidential race to D+29 in Fox’s latest generic ballot survey. That will make a difference across Florida, where seven races shift towards Democrats, including the 25th District (held by Jared Moskowitz (D), from Toss-up to Lean D), and the 27th District (held by María Elvira Salazar (R), from Likely R to Lean R). It also impacts Texas, where the 34th District, held by Vicente Gonzalez (D), moves from Toss-up to Lean D. Republicans are running strong campaigns in many of these districts, but if the Dems’ generic ballot advantage lasts, the party’s ceiling could get higher. Governor: Texas and Alaska drift away from the GOP Data centers continue to play a major role in gubernatorial races across the country, especially in Ohio, where Fox’s Madison Alworth spoke to voters about the costs of data center construction yesterday, and in Texas, where incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott faces his toughest re-election challenge yet. Abbott’s competitor, Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has put the issue at the forefront of both of their campaigns. Yesterday, Abbott widened his moratorium on data centers, with the construction of new centers now "effectively halted" until at least December. The governor has important structural advantages as he seeks a fourth term, but polls keep showing a close race. Texas moves from Likely R to Lean R. Finally, to Alaska, where new polling shows a close race for Senate, and what at first glance looks like a wide-open race for governor, with the Democrat ahead of three Republican candidates. If more Democrats mark their second, third and fourth choices than Republicans, it could hurt the GOP’s chances of holding on to the 49th state. It moves from Lean R to Toss-up.

articles.title: Pentagon unveils battlefield test to ensure new generals are warfighters – not Washington bureaucrats
articles.summary: Pete Hegseth's Pentagon overhaul introduces wargame-style assessments requiring senior officers to solve combat problems before earning a star.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The Pentagon is raising the bar on who gets promoted to general by rolling out a new battlefield-style assessment requiring senior officers to demonstrate how they would solve complex military problems. It's the most significant change in decades for how future generals for every branch are selected. Internal documents obtained by Fox News Digital show every military service has developed its own version of the new Joint Warfighting Evaluation (JWE), a standardized assessment intended to measure operational planning, decision-making and leadership under simulated combat conditions. The Pentagon says the assessment will supplement existing performance evaluations and become an additional metric considered by promotion boards beginning with the fiscal year 2027 cycle. The effort grew out of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's push to overhaul military evaluations and promotions, with a focus on identifying officers who can perform in combat rather than simply build strong career records. PENTAGON FIRES BACK AFTER MARK KELLY ACCUSES PETE HEGSETH OF TARGETING WOMEN AND BLACK MILITARY OFFICERS "People figure out they don't have to be the best at their job, they have to be the best at making sure their boss thinks they're the best," Stu Scheller, the senior Pentagon adviser leading the effort, told Fox News Digital. "And those are actually two very different things." Under the current system, officers accumulate evaluations from their superiors throughout their careers that become a central part of the record considered by promotion boards. 'WOKE' MILITARY ACADEMIES TARGETED IN NEW BLUEPRINT FOR SWEEPING WARFIGHTING OVERHAUL "Right now in our current system, we have people that are very good at navigating their careers," Scheller said. "We have very good, I want to be clear, very good military personnel and leaders across the military, but there isn't a stand-alone function that can truly assess the best military commanders on the battlefield." Scheller said these performance reports will remain the "bedrock" of promotion decisions, while the JWE will give boards a separate measure of how well an officer can solve the kinds of military problems they could face in command. What that assessment looks like will vary by service. The Pentagon has developed six versions — one for each of the five military services and another through the Joint Staff — ranging from online simulations to hours-long, in-person wargames, the documents reviewed by Fox News Digital detail. In some versions, officers will be presented with a military problem and forced to make decisions as an AI-powered adversary reacts to their moves. Another will bring officers into a war college for an in-person wargame, where evaluators will watch how they respond as an enemy counters their decisions in real time. "You make a move, enemy makes a move, how I react based on a time environment," Scheller said. The service plans obtained by Fox News Digital show just how different the evaluations will be. The Army plans to put roughly 900 eligible colonels through a remote written assessment followed by a digital wargame, while roughly 1,330 Air Force colonels will take a two-hour online analysis test followed by a one-hour interactive simulation. The Space Force will use the same basic format for roughly 125 officers. The Navy's version is considerably more intensive. Roughly 308 captains in the unrestricted line and information warfare communities will travel to the Naval War College for a three-hour written assessment followed by a two- to three-hour wargame. The Marine Corps plans an eight-hour remote evaluation for up to 175 colonels using an AI-enabled platform that combines written assessments with situational judgment tests. Scheller cautioned that none of the exercises can perfectly recreate the pressures of actual combat and said the Pentagon expects to change the assessments as it learns what works. "Ultimately, no matter how good we get at this, there's no one task that's gonna perfectly replicate war," he said. "We're not trying to come up with the perfect solution right out the gate." COMMANDING GENERAL OF THE US ARMY IN EUROPEAN AND AFRICAN THEATER IS UNEXPECTEDLY STEPPING DOWN Scheller stressed that the Pentagon is not replacing the existing promotion system. Performance reports and the rest of an officer's career record will continue to account for the bulk of the evaluation, while the JWE will provide promotion boards with an additional data point. How heavily that new data point will be weighted has not yet been decided. "The secretary still has judgment based on how it will be weighted in the board, so we haven't determined," Scheller said. "We're kind of waiting to see how well this thing is rolled out." The first real test will come next year. Eligible O-6s will undergo the evaluations between roughly February and June 2027, Scheller said, ahead of the services' O-7 promotion boards between July and September. The Pentagon plans to study the results from that first cycle before determining how much influence the JWE should have on future promotion boards and how the assessments should evolve for the following year, according to the internal documents. The new evaluation is the latest step in a broader overhaul of how the Pentagon selects, evaluates and retains its senior military leaders under Hegseth. Hegseth told hundreds of generals and admirals last year that the military's promotion system was being "thoroughly reexamined," pledging to promote top performers faster, push out poor performers more quickly and turn evaluations, military education and field exercises into meaningful tests rather than "box checks." He has also moved to shrink the upper ranks themselves, ordering a 20% reduction in active-duty four-star positions and a broader 10% cut in general and flag officer positions as part of a restructuring of military commands. And Hegseth has taken a more direct role in deciding who receives a star. Earlier this year, he removed several Navy captains from a list of officers selected by a promotion board for one-star admiral after previously intervening in an Army brigadier general promotion list. The Pentagon has said promotions under Hegseth will be based on merit. Meanwhile, the unusual interventions have drawn criticism and concern from some lawmakers, military officers and outside analysts worried about political influence over the traditionally service-driven process. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The changes have come alongside significant turnover at the top of the military. Trump and Hegseth have removed or replaced a number of senior leaders since the beginning of the administration, including former Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. CQ Brown and former Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Lisa Franchetti. Hegseth also forced out Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George this year before the scheduled end of his term.

articles.title: Trump weighed removing all press from White House: Report
articles.summary: President Trump has reportedly mulled whether to move the entire White House press corps from the building to another nearby location. Trump has weighed the idea on multiple occasions during both terms, The Wall Street Journal reported, and he brought the idea up again as recently as within the last month as his frustration has…
articles.body:
President Trump has reportedly mulled whether to move the entire White House press corps from the building to another nearby location.

Trump has weighed the idea on multiple occasions during both terms, The Wall Street Journal reported, and he brought the idea up again as recently as within the last month as his frustration has grown with the media coverage he is receiving.

Some administration officials warned the president against the move , according to the Journal, which was told by a White House official that Trump had no imminent plans to remove press from the building.

The report comes just days after Trump barred three top news outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — from the White House over their coverage of him.

The outlets sued the administration over the move on Monday, and the TV pool typically covering the president boycotted coverage the same day over the ban.

Trump’s move has been widely condemned by press freedom groups, elected Democrats and even some conservative commentators.

Under Trump, the White House has shifted the way the press operates while covering the president, making changes to the briefing room and scaling back the number of wire services traveling with the president.

The president last year also banned The Associated Press from certain White House spaces over its refusal to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America,” a move the wire service sued over and won .

Trump has long railed against mainstream media coverage of his administration, most recently the Iran war and issues relating to the economy, key points of emphasis for voters ahead of November’s midterm elections.

articles.title: The IRS’s cruel new proposal weaponizes civil lights law against itself
articles.summary: It is a power grab that should alarm everyone, regardless of where you stand on affirmative action.
articles.body:
What the IRS proposed Sept. 3 is not enforcement. It is a power grab that should alarm everyone, regardless of where you stand on affirmative action.

I spent five years as an IRS attorney enforcing the tax rules that govern private schools. These new regulations propose to strip tax exemption — and with it the charitable deduction, access to foundation grants, and in many cases state tax exemptions — from any private school operating any race-conscious program for any purpose. The agency’s estimates put the affected universe at 18,000 institutions and 750,000 students.

The deeper problem is not the impact on private schools. It is what the IRS claims the executive branch can do to any private institution the administration opposes. The IRS asserts the power to take a Supreme Court precedent, declare it reflects national policy and through the tax code impose that policy on private actors the precedent does not reach.

That is not enforcement of existing law. That is the creation of new legislative and executive power the court never granted and Congress never authorized.

Some history is needed. In 1983 the Supreme Court decided Bob Jones University v. United States , upholding the IRS’s revocation of tax exemption from a university that practiced racial segregation. That case is the legal foundation of the current regulations. But it also exposes their fatal flaw.

The Court in Bob Jones did not give the IRS open-ended power to define national policy through the tax code. It authorized the IRS in that specific case because all three branches of government had converged on the same prohibition over decades.

Congress had passed the Civil Rights Acts and the courts had decided Brown v. Board of Education . Presidents of both parties had enforced desegregation. In Bob Jones, Justice Lewis Powell wrote separately to warn that without that deep democratic agreement the IRS could become exactly what we are seeing today: a weapon aimed at ideological opponents.

Here the convergence runs the other way. Congress has never legislated against race-conscious remediation. The IRS itself explicitly protected minority-favoring scholarship and admissions programs for over the last 50 years. The administration is not implementing a democratic consensus. It is claiming the power to create one by decree.

The administration’s legal theory rests entirely on Students for Fair Admissions , the 2023 Supreme Court decision striking down race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina. But that decision was decided under the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act . Both apply to government actors and recipients of federal funding. The court was not declaring a new national policy binding on every private school in America but only resolving a specific legal dispute about specific programs at specific institutions.

The IRS does not explain how a constitutional holding about university admission policies becomes a tax exemption standard for every private school in the country. It has simply asserted it.

The stakes here are not limited to the institutions currently under attack. Every tax-exempt organization in America — including universities, hospitals, foundations, advocacy organizations, churches — now operates in a legal environment where the executive branch claims the power to define fundamental public policy through the tax code based on judicial decisions it selects.

Institutions whose entire mission is remedying the effects of historical discrimination face the particular cruelty of having that mission turned against them by the very legal doctrine designed to protect it.

Whatever you think of affirmative action, ask yourself what a future administration might do with the same theory. The answer should worry everyone.

These regulations should be withdrawn. If the administration believes Students for Fair Admissions requires this result, it should go to Congress and make that argument. Congress can act. Congress can be held accountable. IRS rulemaking cannot.

This is not enforcement of existing law. It is the assertion of new power dressed as a legal obligation. The courts should reject it.

Philip Hackney is a professor of Law at the University of Pittsburgh School of Law.

Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard
Title VI of the Civil Rights Act

articles.title: White House outlines Trump talking points ahead of high-profile UN speech
articles.summary: The White House outlined President Trump’s address to the United Nations on Tuesday, when he is expected to touch on a number of hot-button issues including the Iran war, drug cartels and the U.S. military presence in Greenland. A White House official told The Hill that in his speech, Trump will lay out his case…
articles.body:
The White House outlined President Trump’s address to the United Nations on Tuesday, when he is expected to touch on a number of hot-button issues including the Iran war, drug cartels and the U.S. military presence in Greenland.

A White House official told The Hill that in his speech, Trump will lay out his case for how he is “using American Power to confront longstanding challenges and reshape the world to America’s benefit.”

Trump will address the nuclear threat from Iran, cartel violence and U.S. interests in Greenland, arguing that his policies on the issues will result in a “much safer and more prosperous world for the American people.”

The official also noted Trump will tout his administration’s efforts to end “violence, instability, and foreign interference” in the Western Hemisphere, as well as highlight his efforts to block the U.N. and other “globalist institutions” from infringing on “American sovereignty or imposing a radical-left wing agenda” on the U.S.

Following his speech, Trump is set to participate in a trilateral signing ceremony to formalize the new security agreement between the U.S, Greenland and Denmark.

Trump’s speech to the body comes as he faces pressure on a number of international fronts, including the war in Iran, which has led to a spike in energy prices in the U.S. and across the world.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that while nothing is scheduled, Trump would be open to meeting with Iranian officials at the international gathering.

Trump is slated to meet with a number of international leaders, including U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

articles.title: SEE IT: Top Dem operative draws line at ‘deplorable’ Hasan Piker after touting party’s ‘big tent’
articles.summary: DNC Chairman Ken Martin calls Hasan Piker's comments "disgusting and deplorable" while distancing Democrats from the controversial streamer.
articles.body: Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin distanced his party from far-left streamer Hasan Piker, calling his past remarks "disgusting and deplorable" while defending Democrats as a "big tent" that encompasses a wide range of political views. "Let me just say that I think it's absolutely disgusting and deplorable the things that Hasan Piker has said," Martin said. "But he does not represent the Democratic Party, and he certainly doesn't represent the viewpoints of almost every one of our candidates and our elected officials." Martin made the remarks after Fox News Digital asked how the party is navigating divisions among Democrats as socialist candidates gain prominence, including Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. RASKIN CALLS PIKER’S RHETORIC 'IRRELEVANT DISTRACTION' AFTER THE STREAMER SAID HE'D VOTE FOR HAMAS OVER ISRAEL "Look, no one should confuse unity with unanimity in the Democratic Party, right?" Martin said. "We are a big tent party. We have lots of different viewpoints and ideas and all sorts of issues." Piker has been scrutinized for a slew of past comments critical of Israel — one of his most controversial comments was claiming that the U.S. "deserved 9/11." Martin previously joined other party leaders and prominent Democrats in condemning rhetoric blaming Jewish Americans for threats and violence, calling it "dangerous, wrong, and antisemitic," but his statement did not name Piker. "Criticizing the policies and actions of the Israeli government is one thing," Martin posted to X last month. "Blaming American Jews for the hatred, threats, and violence directed at them is something else entirely. It is dangerous, wrong, and antisemitic." The comments come as El-Sayed, who campaigned with Piker during Michigan's Democratic primary, has sought to distance himself from the streamer as Republicans make their association a midterm attack line. EL-SAYED GRILLED ON PIKER, ISRAEL AND SOCIALIST TIES AFTER MIKE ROGERS SKIPS SENATE DEBATE Martin also called out Republicans for cutting the House’s September session short and leaving Capitol Hill weeks before the midterm elections, telling Fox News Digital there is crucial legislative work that will be left unfinished. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week that he was canceling votes scheduled last week and sent lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess. Johnson has defended the decision, saying the House had "done its work." "Republicans… they're afraid to actually come to Washington for a whole host of reasons, right?" Martin said. "They've recessed saying mission accomplished six weeks early when they could actually do something to help the American people." "What the hell are they doing? Where are they going? You know what, Democrats are here. We're ready to work. We are ready to pass legislation that actually helps get people a chance, an opportunity, a chance to get ahead. Where the hell are the Republicans?" WHY THE HOUSE LET OUT EARLY IS A MATTER OF DEBATE AFTER JOHNSON SAYS CHAMBER HAS 'DONE ITS WORK' Martin also predicted Democrats would win control of both chambers in November as the elections inch closer, with roughly six weeks until Americans vote to determine which party will control the Senate and the House. "Mark my words right here," Martin said. "You heard it here first, right? 47 days left. The Democratic Party is going to take control of the House back, and we're going to control the Senate back, and we're not going to screw around like these Republicans have." articles.title: Jennings: Trump ‘unlikely to prevail in court’ on press ban, has ‘less reach’
articles.summary: Scott Jennings said Monday that President Trump’s decision to ban MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House is “unlikely to prevail in court” after the three outlets announced they will mount a legal challenge. “It seems to me the net result of this has been he has less reach and his message is…
articles.body:
Scott Jennings said Monday that President Trump’s decision to ban MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House is “unlikely to prevail in court” after the three outlets announced they will mount a legal challenge .

“It seems to me the net result of this has been he has less reach and his message is not going to get out as much,” Jennings said on CNN’s “Newsnight.”

“If this sort of becomes the way it is, he will be seen and heard by fewer people, which I think is actually a net negative since he’s his own best spokesperson and his own best press secretary,” he continued, adding that the president’s exchanges with journalists in the Oval Office “works to his advantage.”

Jennings has been floated as a top contender to replace former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down from the role at the end of August.

The conservative political commentator previously served as a special assistant to former President Bush and as an adviser to Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.). As a CNN contributor, Jennings has frequently defended Trump’s actions during his second term during his on-air appearances.

After Trump’s announced ban, TV networks pulled out of the White House press pool in solidarity. The presidential pool, which consists of five major networks, is responsible for recording and dispersing video footage from the president’s events for general news coverage use.

Pool members Fox News Media, ABC News, CBS News, NBC News and CNN said in a rare joint statement that “the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.”

“No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” they added.

At a ribbon cutting event aired by Newsmax on Monday, Trump stood in front of a group of construction workers and spoke to the camera. However, the president’s comments were not audible because the pool was not there to capture audio at the event.

The president defended his ban on Monday morning, denying in a Truth Social post that the move amounted to an “assault on the Free Press.”

“It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” he wrote. “It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

It is unclear what prompted the president to institute this ban.

articles.title: Dem reactions within moments of Austin ICE shooting spark viral outrage locally, online: 'Disqualifying'
articles.summary: Austin Texas Democrats face backlash for attacking ICE before any investigation into the shooting of a suspected illegal immigrant was completed.
articles.body: Democrats in Austin, Texas, are facing criticism both online and from a retired cop who spoke to Fox News Digital after rushing to attack Immigration and Customs Enforcement moments after a suspected illegal immigrant was shot before any investigation had taken place. An ICE officer shot a man in Austin on Sunday and almost immediately, before basic facts had been established in the case, and before the man had been identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, elected Democrats in Austin were speaking out against ICE, including Rep. Greg Casar, Councilman Mike Siegel, and Mayor Kirk Watson. "It is awful that this war has come to our doorstep," Casar, a member of the progressive Squad caucus, said during a Sunday press conference in a clip that was highlighted by the White House Rapid Response account on X. "And as the mayor said, unfortunately it is not a surprise. Just a few weeks ago as we saw the ICE surge come to Austin, especially to north central Austin, I and others said that ICE needed to leave before someone was shot like in Minneapolis or like in Corpus Christi or like in Chicago, and that day is here and so I think the message remains that for Austin to be safe, ICE should end its surge here in our community." BRANDON GILL UNLOADS ON DEMOCRATS OVER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH RAPING TEEN: 'COLLATERAL DAMAGE' Casar and his fellow Democrats quickly sparked viral social media criticism from conservatives accusing the left of selective outrage when it comes to crime, particularly illegal immigrant crime. "Where was the outcry from this guy last fall when an illegal alien in Texas used a machete to behead a man in front of his spouse and child?" Tricia McLaughlin, former assistant secretary of Homeland Security for public affairs, posted on X. "The perpetrator reportedly kicked the head of the victim ‘around like a soccer ball.’ " "There it is," Townhall’s Amy Curtis posted on X. "The Democrats want no immigration laws. They want to destroy this nation. Remember this in November." "This sort of rhetoric should be disqualifying for any elected official," Texas Republican State Rep. Andy Hopper posted on X. "You cannot faithfully take the oath of office and be for open borders. " Dennis Farris, president of the Austin Police Retired Officers Association, told Fox News Digital he expects that kind of rhetoric from Casar and Siegel but was surprised to hear Mayor Watson rush to place blame on ICE both in the press conference and on social media. ‘OUT OF CONTROL’ KILLINGS IN SPANBERGER’S VIRGINIA REACH ‘INSANE’ POINT AS MIGRANT CHARGED IN STABBING SPREE "With Casar, it didn't surprise me, that’s Greg Casar, he's a bomb thrower, he's been a bomb thrower and he's been a reactionary known for shooting his mouth off before he has all the facts," Farris said. "He did that when he was on the city council. He did it in the Mike Ramos shooting. That’s just Greg Casar, He's known for his theatrics." "I've known the mayor a long time, consider the mayor a friend, I was really shocked at how visceral his reaction was, he's usually a lot more measured," Farris said. "I can understand being upset but the way he reacted, I think, raised the temperature in Austin because he is the one that he is, the leader, right? He is the city leader. He's the mayor. He's the one supposed to be trying to keep things calm and I think his reaction yesterday made it worse." Watson’s post was "ratioed" on social media, yielding far more negative comments and quote tweets than positive ones, with locals and internet users accusing him of fanning the flames before the facts were known. "Honestly shocking Mayor @KirkPWatson would issue this sort of statement knowing full well the investigation has barely started, Hope he’s not about to make an Adler-esque 2nd term turn," prominent Austin attorney Adam Loewy posted on X, referencing former Austin Mayor Steve Adler who presided over the 2020 George Floyd rioting in the city. Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of Casar, Watson, and Siegel for comment. Farris rejected Democrat claims that ICE is "surging" in Austin and said that federal immigration authorities, whether ICE or INS, have been conducting deportations in Austin for decades without any fanfare. "They've been arresting people that were in the country illegally and I think what we're seeing here is that the reaction to it is because of Trump, it's the Trump administration doing it and it's just another way to dislike the president for whatever reason you want to dislike him for," Farris said. articles.title: Jon Stewart rips Trump’s media ban: ‘Have you tried presidenting better?’
articles.summary: Jon Stewart is railing against President Trump’s White House ban on three media organizations, saying the “authoritarian crackdown” won’t bring down fuel prices or improve the job he’s doing as commander in chief. Trump said on Friday in a Truth Social post that he was banning MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House “as…
articles.body:
Jon Stewart is railing against President Trump’s White House ban on three media organizations, saying the “authoritarian crackdown” won’t bring down fuel prices or improve the job he’s doing as commander in chief.

Trump said on Friday in a Truth Social post that he was banning MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

The trio of news outlets said in a Monday joint statement that they are filing a lawsuit against the Trump administration “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”

On Monday’s “The Daily Show,” Stewart ripped Trump for the move.

“Have you tried presidenting better?” Stewart asked in his monologue on the Comedy Central show.

“You could ban the press, or you could be a better f—ing president,” he said.

“I mean, give the press something to work with,” Stewart continued, before highlighting the rising gas prices across the country amid the U.S. war in Iran.

“Oh, here’s a positive story: I never thought my car could take $140 worth of gas in such a small tank. I had no idea,” he quipped.

“And not for nothing, have we ever had a president just flat out in the Oval Office come out against the Constitution?” Stewart said.

“What kind of a sick country doesn’t allow unlimited warrantless search and seizure? I mean, that’s not the North Korea I grew up in,” Stewart said as he imitated Trump.

“Are you talking about my authoritarian crackdown?” Stewart, continuing to mock the president, told the audience.

“He gives no f—s. He doesn’t even respect us enough to pretend he’s bound by our Constitution,” the 63-year-old comedian said.

Stewart then brought in “Daily Show” correspondent Desi Lydic, who in the satirical sketch said she was reporting from the Oval Office after disguising herself as a golden cherub and blending into the embellishments adorning the doorway in the White House room.

“What’s been the effect of this media ban so far?” Stewart asked Lydic.

“Well, it’s been surprising and immediate: Since banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico, gas prices have plummeted to $1.98,” Lydic cracked.

“Are you saying the ban on the press actually worked?” Stewart, feigning shock, replied.

“Yeah, it turns out Trump was absolutely right,” Lydic said, adding, “CNN and MS NOW were the only reason everything was bad.”

articles.title: O’Reilly: ‘Republicans can’t survive the anger that people are feeling’ on spending

Appearing on NewsNation, host Leland Vittert asked O’Reilly if remarks made by Republican candidates in battleground elections who are calling for an end to the Iran war as grocery…
articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Monday said Republicans cannot survive the anger people are feeling about the ongoing affordability crisis ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

Appearing on NewsNation, host Leland Vittert asked O’Reilly if remarks made by Republican candidates in battleground elections who are calling for an end to the Iran war as grocery and energy prices continue to rise were correct.

“Theoretically, they’re right, but you can make a Munich argument about looking the other way when a terrorist has a nuclear weapon, is trying to get one,” O’Reilly said. “You can make that argument, but a realistic argument is enough.”

“Republicans can’t survive the anger that people are feeling when they spend as much money as they’re spending. Can’t survive it,” he continued.

The commentator stated he expected “something to happen shortly” that will alter Americans’ views on Iran, and “that’s positive to the United States.” O’Reilly was unclear what that would be.

“But I don’t think it can hang on much longer,” he concluded.

His comments were in response to Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate candidate in Iowa, who on Monday linked the war in Iran to rising prices in the U.S. Her move was echoed by former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee in Michigan’s Senate race, who said “Michigan families can’t afford to wait” for the Iran war to reach its conclusion, calling for an end to the conflict.

President Trump has defended the war effort in the face of rising prices, saying at a rally on Wednesday that high costs were “a very inexpensive price to pay for” the Iran war.

“But that’s going to come tumbling down. That’s going to be like rocket ships in reverse,” he added.

The division within the GOP comes as Democrats make the cost of living a core issue going into the midterm elections.

The U.S.-Israeli conflict in Iran has caused energy prices to skyrocket worldwide, pushing the national average price of gas to $4.47 per gallon as of Tuesday, according to AAA . Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping lane for oil exports, is the primary cause of higher prices in recent months.

articles.title: Trump ‘definitely backed into a corner’: Former press secretary
articles.summary: Former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham said Monday that President Trump is in a tight spot with his restrictions on media outlets. “Well, he’s definitely backed into a corner, but he’s not going to admit that. So, to answer your question, yes, he’s going to continue to double down, which I think he already…
articles.body:
Former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham said Monday that President Trump is in a tight spot with his restrictions on media outlets.

“Well, he’s definitely backed into a corner, but he’s not going to admit that. So, to answer your question, yes, he’s going to continue to double down, which I think he already did with that post talking about, you know, that they’re going to appeal this — the case that’s going on Wednesday,” Grisham told CNN’s Erin Burnett on “OutFront.”

“I think he’s going to rely on appealing until he gets to the Supreme Court, thinking that maybe they’re going to be the ones who kind of side with him,” she added.

Trump denied on Monday that he was “instituting an assault” against the press after he barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House over their coverage.

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” Trump said in a Truth Social post, stating his administration was “instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS.”

“It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” he continued.

All three outlets are now suing the White House to regain their access. They’ve been supported by much of the rest of the White House media, including the network pool reporters, who have said they will not provide a video pool for Trump until CNN’s access is restored. CNN is one of the “five families” that provide the video pool, along with NBC, CBS, ABC and Fox News.

The outlets banned by Trump are widely expected to win in court on constitutional grounds.

“They have drawn a great Judge, for them,” Trump said of U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee who will oversee the case. Trump vowed to appeal any decision that goes against him.

“In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World,” Trump said on Truth Social.

The president could not be heard in live footage during a ribbon-cutting ceremony Monday debuting the new South Lawn helipad at the White House.

While the president could be seen cutting a ribbon on a walkway for the helipad, as well as talking with construction workers, his words were not audible.

A host for the conservative outlet Newsmax noted in their coverage of the event that a microphone wasn’t there because the pool cameras were not at the event.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: What good is a nurse’s union that spends nurses’ money to make their jobs harder?
articles.summary: If the union collecting these workers’ dues will not help them enter the future, they should reject the union.
articles.body:
On August 27, National Nurses United, the nation’s largest nurses’ union, staged coordinated protests across eight American cities .

Were they picketing for better pay, safer staffing or less paperwork?

No. They coordinated the protests to demand that hospitals cancel contracts with Palantir, whose systems help schedule staff, manage records, and cut the administrative load that burns people out. The union marched its members into the street to stop hospitals from adopting tools that could put their members back at the bedside, in the roles they had trained for.

The same pattern is appearing wherever new tools threaten a dues structure. When the International Longshoremen’s Association went to the bargaining table, it passed over retraining and a share of the gains from a more productive port. It instead demanded an absolute ban on automated cranes and gates and was prepared to choke the country’s supply chain to get it.

In California, SEIU Local 1000 filed grievances seeking a consultative veto over the state’s new artificial intelligence tools, on the theory that a technology that makes a public employee more useful should be slowed or barred. Longshoremen keep American shelves stocked and factories running. State workers can keep the public’s business moving. Both could use better tools to make their jobs more efficient and productive. So why are unions fighting to stop making life better for their members?

American workers have met new tools before, and they have come out ahead. When the telephone displaced the telegraph, the operators who mastered the new instrument built an occupation that had not existed a decade earlier. The assembly line broke the old craft shops and produced the wages and household stability that became the American middle class. The personal computer emptied typing pools and ledger rooms, then opened an information economy whose job titles would have been nonsense in 1975.

Each time, the country grew richer. The men and women who met the change on their own terms grew with it.

Artificial intelligence presents us with the next change. Used well, it frees people from administrative arbitrage that steals time from the real work itself. Productivity on that scale means better conditions, better pay, and a better life for people who do the work. But too many unions are meeting the moment with fear and obstinacy, rather than embracing the future.

The economy is moving without them. Research from the Mercatus Center finds that since early 2024, solo business formation and self-employment have risen 27 percent in the sectors most exposed to artificial intelligence. One person can now do what once required a team, a lease, and a firm’s entire support apparatus.

Union officials, rather than finding ways to make work easier for their members, are using members’ dues for their own purposes. According to the Commonwealth Foundation , the four largest public-sector unions spent more than $700 million on political activity in the 2021-2022 cycle, nearly 96 percent of which went to Democratic candidates and causes. Teachers, nurses, clerks, and tradesmen paid those dues in the hope of a better wage and a safer floor, but the money financed a partisan operation. A union that spends its money on elections rather than on the people who earned them has already shown those people what it thinks they are for.

But further, consider what these unions are campaigning for. Artificial intelligence is already here, and we can use it to make life better. Nurses who learn the new systems will spend fewer hours on paperwork and drudgery and more hours caring for patients — the way most medical professionals would prefer.

Likewise, the dockworker who masters a modern terminal will keep American commerce moving and will be paid for a scarce skill. The public employee who learns to use AI will have better tools to serve the public faster. If the union collecting these workers’ dues will not help them enter that future, they should reject the union.

American workers have always been equal to what came next when they were told the truth about it and given a fair chance to meet it. They built this country by embracing change, working hard, and leaving the world as a better place than the one they had been handed. That work is waiting for them again. Any union that asks them to fear it has forfeited the right to take their money and speak in their name.

Gene Hamilton is a Senior Advisor to the Coalition to Protect American Workers. He previously served as Deputy White House Counsel to President Trump.

articles.body:
Vice President Vance and Dr. Mehmet Oz, who leads the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), are expected to announce a new crackdown Tuesday on alleged fraud in Affordable Care Act insurance exchanges.

The administration plans to cancel subsidy payments tied to 760,000 accounts it says are fraudulent, unauthorized or otherwise ineligible, according to The Wall Street Journal . Officials estimate the move will save taxpayers roughly $2.2 billion.

CMS is also expected to cut off hundreds of insurance agents and brokers accused of improperly enrolling people in coverage. The move is the latest action from the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud , which Vance leads as President Trump’s “ fraud czar .”

The event is scheduled to begin at 11:30 a.m. EDT.

articles.title: El-Sayed on Carlson praise: MAGA ‘eating itself’

Mike Rogers. El-Sayed was asked Monday about Carlson’s comments on the race earlier this month, when the former Fox News host said he “wouldn’t vote…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) said President Trump’s MAGA movement is “eating itself” after conservative commentator Tucker Carlson praised the progressive while tearing into his GOP opponent , former Rep. Mike Rogers.

El-Sayed was asked Monday about Carlson’s comments on the race earlier this month, when the former Fox News host said he “wouldn’t vote for Mike Rogers at gunpoint” and propped up El-Sayed’s “Trumpian” campaign.

“Look, Tucker and I don’t agree on much, but we definitely agree on what he just said,” the Senate hopeful said in an appearance on CNN’s “OutFront” with host Erin Burnett. “I think what you’re seeing here is MAGA eating itself.”

He argued that some supporters of Trump’s “ America First ” movement were turning against Republicans who they believe are abandoning its principles, particularly on foreign policy as the U.S.’s unpopular war in Iran nears the seven-month mark.

“Those who believe in the ideas — the idea that we should have America first, that we shouldn’t go to wars that we shouldn’t be fighting, those who believe in just basic principles,” the progressive added.

El-Sayed, who narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens (Mich.) in the Democratic primary for the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D), accused Rogers of shifting his positions to remain aligned with Trump.

“Folks are turning on people like Mike Rogers because Mike Rogers was a neocon, and then he decried Donald Trump when Donald Trump came to power,” he continued. “Now, he’s willing to do whatever Donald Trump tells him to do, so long as Donald Trump is happy with him.”

The former GOP lawmaker, who is endorsed by Trump, recently called for a swift end to the U.S. war in Iran after previously backing the president’s handling of the conflict. His campaign cited the economic impact of the war, including surging fuel prices tied to Tehran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

El-Sayed stressed that he does not believe Carlson, a former Trump ally , was making a formal endorsement of his campaign, but rather a “nonendorsement for Mike Rogers” or “an anti-endorsement” against his GOP opponent.

The progressive added that Carlson’s words were “less about me. It’s more about Mike Rogers, and it’s more about recognizing that I am going to be principled — whatever it takes.”

El-Sayed and Rogers will face off in November for the Senate seat, which the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates as a “toss-up.”

articles.title: Trump tells CNN’s Collins ‘you shouldn’t be here’ on way into UN
articles.summary: President Trump on Tuesday brushed aside questions from CNN Chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins amid his push to block the network and two other outlets from covering the White House. During the president’s arrival at the UN General Assembly meeting in New York City Tuesday morning, Trump said he was “surprised” to see the…
articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday brushed aside questions from CNN Chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins amid his push to block the network and two other outlets from covering the White House.

During the president’s arrival at the UN General Assembly meeting in New York City Tuesday morning, Trump said he was “surprised” to see the journalist, according to video footage shared by CSPAN.

“You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to be covering me,” Trump said as Collins shouted a question about new CNN polling that showed rising dissatisfaction among the American public with his administration’s military operations against Iran.

Following this exchange with the president, Collins noted in an appearance on “CNN News Central” that she and other reporters present were credentialed under the UN.

Collins added that the network “never said we were not going to cover the president.”

“We will continue to cover the president and his speech and as he meets with world leaders today, just not with a TV camera from one of the five major networks in the room,” she added.

On Monday, CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit to challenge the president’s decision to revoke White House press credentials for the three news outlets. It is not clear what led the president to issue this ban.

In the filing , attorneys for the three outlets accused Trump of targeting them because he “dislikes the content of their coverage of him and his administration.”

“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawyers wrote in the complaint.

TV networks pulled their participation in the presidential pool in solidarity with the impacted outlets. The pool travels with the president and is responsible for capturing and sharing footage from his public appearances.

In a rare joint statement, pool members Fox News Media, ABC News, CBS News, NBC News and CNN said, “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.”

“No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” they added.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the president’s media ban during a Monday morning appearance on NBC News’s “TODAY” show.

“I don’t think the White House is saying they’re not able to cover the President,” Rubio told host Craig Melvin.

“What he is arguing is, why should I have these people? What right do they have to be embedded in this building?” the secretary added. “They can cover the White House; they just can’t have a desk there.”

articles.title: California senators call for probe into Trump administration election operation
articles.summary: Sens. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) on Sunday called on California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) to launch a probe into a whistleblower’s allegations that the Trump administration attempted to search through the state’s voting records. The senators wrote in a letter to Bonta that on Sept. 8, a whistleblower disclosed that the…
articles.body:
Sens. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) on Sunday called on California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) to launch a probe into a whistleblower’s allegations that the Trump administration attempted to search through the state’s voting records.

The senators wrote in a letter to Bonta that on Sept. 8, a whistleblower disclosed that the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) subdivision, the Fraud and Detection and National Security Directorate (FDNS), were assigned to an “‘unlawful voter initiative’ using highly questionable data and methods to identify purported unlawful voters.”

“DHS and USCIS training materials admit these investigations will include U.S. citizens, some of whom will have federal law enforcement records created against them based on questionable data and rushed reviews by officers held to quotas,” Padilla, the top Democrat on the Senate committee overseeing federal elections, and Schiff stated.

The Hill has reached out to DHS for comment.

The whistleblower claimed that USCIS personnel were directed to access voter information without authorization, violating state law, according to the senators. They added that these quotas demanded that USCIS personnel investigate 40 subjects a day with agency leaders tracking their output “in an attempt to complete this rushed investigation by Sept. 12.”

“The Trump administration appears to be undertaking this rushed effort to find –– or manufacture –– evidence for its baseless election conspiracy theories of widespread voter fraud ahead of the 2026 midterm elections,” the California Democrats wrote, adding that accusing naturalized citizens of being “unlawful voters” will have “serious consequences for Californians.”

Padilla and Schiff alleged that USCIS personnel were told to misrepresent themselves to access the voter data, and claimed that DHS handed the voter data to FDNS officers. They said the whistleblower was “dismissed” by agency leaders.

“Considering California’s strong protections surrounding the use of voter registration information and [personally identifiable information], we believe this disclosure merits a review by your office to determine what actions are necessary and appropriate to protect California voters,” the senators wrote to Bonta.

Padilla said in a statement that following the whistleblower’s disclosure, he and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) last week called on DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and USCIS Director Joseph Edlow to halt the “unlawful voter initiative” and update Congress on the initiative’s activities.

The 30-page disclosure from the whistleblower alleged that employees were ordered to search voter data despite concerns that they could be violating state law, and they were assured individuals would not be held liable, possibly indicating that the agency was “aware that the activity may be illegal.”

The Trump administration previously sought voter data from several states, and the Department of Justice (DOJ) sued those that did not comply. A federal judge dismissed the DOJ’s suit against California in January, calling the government’s request “unprecedented and illegal.”

articles.title: Trump finds rampant noncitizen voting in … Ken Paxton’s Texas
articles.summary: A report from the U.S. Census Bureau alleging thousands of noncitizen voters in the 2020 election has prompted questions regarding whether Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and the federal government are failing to prosecute such individuals or are presenting inaccurate data.
articles.body:
Ken Paxton, call your office! President Trump has a report from the U.S. Census Bureau that purports to expose the states with the largest number of noncitizen voters in the 2020 election.

Texas comes in second with 2,500 alleged noncitizen voters — and the bureau says there’s more to come.

If true, state Attorney General Paxton needs to explain why more alleged noncitizen voters haven’t been charged.

Just a few weeks ago, at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Trump claimed Ken Paxton was the best state attorney general in history. But how can that be if Texas and the federal government have failed to charge all those alleged noncitizen voters with voter fraud ?

On Aug. 18, the Census Bureau released an unusual report titled, “Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election, a Beginning Analysis.” But there are problems.

First, it’s not the bureau’s mission or expertise to cover election integrity and voter fraud, so why is it spending time and resources doing that?

And then there’s the timing. The report claims to be a “beginning analysis.” Of the nearly 160 million voters who cast ballots in the 2020 general election, the bureau’s “beginning analysis readily determined with high confidence that over 128 million of these voter records represented citizens, and that over 24,000 of these voter records represented noncitizens at the time of the election.”

But the report is incomplete. It says, “Over 32 million voter records remain to be analyzed.”

If some 20 percent of voter records still needed to be analyzed, why not wait until the job is finished to release a report? The findings, if true, aren’t going to change the 2020 election. Was the purpose to try and validate Trump’s claim that the 2020 election was stolen in order to justify interfering in the coming midterm election?

The report also rounds the numbers for every state. California, with 4,300, has the largest number of alleged noncitizen voters. Texas is second with 2,500. Third-place Florida has 1,800, followed by New York with 1,700. Providing rounded, rather than specific, numbers implies a lack of confidence in the data.

In contrast, the government did provide specific numbers in a July 16 report. Trump delivered a much-hyped nationwide press conference stating emphatically that, based on a “preliminary review,” the Department of Homeland Security had identified more than 250,000 noncitizen voters in just four states — California, New Jersey, Nevada and Pennsylvania. California allegedly had 190,832 noncitizen voters.

Why was the government’s July claim of 190,832 alleged California noncitizen voters so much larger than its August report citing 4,300?

Note that while the press release said these were “potential” noncitizen voters, neither Trump nor Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin mentioned that point in their public statements, making it sound as if these were confirmed noncitizens who actually voted.

Paxton’s office has initiated voter-fraud charges a number of times during his 10 years as attorney general. And he has occasionally worked with local and federal law enforcement officials to arrest and charge people. For example, last year Paxton announced he was investigating 33 noncitizens for voting in the 2024 election. And the Department of Justice just announced it had charged seven noncitizens in Texas “for unlawfully voting in federal elections or falsely claiming United States citizenship.”

Though we don’t know the outcome of these charges, a relatively small number of noncitizens do register to vote, and a smaller number even try to cast a ballot — sometimes successfully. Of course, New Jersey recently announced it had erroneously registered some 6,000 noncitizens.

But the number of noncitizen voters isn’t in the thousands, as the Trump administration claims. It’s not even in the hundreds in Texas. The numbers are relatively small given 17.7 million Texas voters . Moreover, most of those charged over the years are for other types of voter-fraud offenses, such as possessing marked mail-in ballots without voter consent.

In contrast to Trump’s grandiose claims of noncitizen voting, the Texas Secretary of State’s Office just announced it had referred 117 cases of “potential noncitizen voting” to Paxton’s office for investigation. The Secretary of State also confirmed that “578 other registered voters flagged last year as potential noncitizens by a federal database are, in fact, U.S. citizens,” according to the Texas Tribune .

Several states have also scoured their voter rolls in recent years, and only a very small number of cases of noncitizen voting were found. For example, Florida found 85, Georgia 139, Ohio 138 and Iowa 35, according to Politifact . Such small numbers undermine Trump’s claim of widespread noncitizen voting.

So, either Paxton and the Justice Department have as yet failed to charge thousands of known noncitizen voters in Texas. Or the Trump administration is releasing unreliable noncitizen-voter data that is at best greatly exaggerated, or at worst just plain false. It can’t be both.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.
